title: Up to Five Cups of Coffee a Day May Benefit Heart Health, AHA Says
excerpt: A new American Heart Association scientific statement finds that moderate coffee consumption is not just safe but may lower the risk of heart disease, stroke, and Type 2 diabetes — though energy drinks are a different story.
body:
• The American Heart Association's new scientific statement, published in Circulation on July 20, concludes that up to 400 mg of caffeine per day — roughly five cups of black coffee — is safe for most adults.
  • Regular coffee consumption of two to five cups daily was linked to a lower risk of Type 2 diabetes, heart disease, heart failure, and stroke.
  • The benefits apply to plain, filtered coffee; unfiltered methods like espresso and French press may raise LDL cholesterol due to a compound called cafestol.
  • Energy drinks and energy shots were distinguished as carrying higher risks of hypertension and arrhythmias, and should not be treated the same as coffee.

What the AHA Found

The American Heart Association published a comprehensive scientific statement on July 20, 2026, in its flagship journal Circulation, reviewing the cumulative evidence on coffee consumption and cardiovascular health. The central finding: drinking up to five eight-ounce cups of caffeinated coffee per day — containing roughly 400 milligrams of caffeine — is generally safe for healthy adults and may confer measurable cardiovascular benefits.

"For people who are already drinking coffee, I think the data is very reassuring that two to five cups per day is not just safe, it may be healthful in terms of lower risk of certain chronic diseases," said Frank Hu, the Fredrick J. Stare Professor of Nutrition and Epidemiology at Harvard's T.H. Chan School of Public Health and a co-author of the statement.

Among the evidence reviewed, a meta-analysis of 28 prospective cohort studies found that consuming 3.5 to 5 cups of coffee daily was associated with a 20% to 30% reduction in Type 2 diabetes risk. Moderate coffee intake was also linked to lower rates of heart failure, stroke, and coronary heart disease.

Why Coffee Is Not Just Caffeine

The health benefits appear to stem not from caffeine alone but from hundreds of bioactive compounds found in coffee beans, particularly polyphenols and chlorogenic acid.

"Coffee contains not just caffeine, but numerous bioactive compounds like polyphenols, which may have health benefits. Studies have shown that the metabolism of the polyphenols by the gut bacteria leads to production of beneficial metabolites, which can reduce oxidative stress and reduce chronic inflammation."

— Frank Hu, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

Chlorogenic acid, one of the most abundant phenolic compounds in coffee, has been shown to reduce glucose absorption and improve glucose metabolism. These benefits were observed in both regular and decaffeinated coffee, suggesting that caffeine is only part of the equation.

Not All Coffee Is Equal

The AHA statement drew important distinctions based on how coffee is prepared and consumed. Filtered coffee and instant coffee showed no association with elevated cholesterol. But unfiltered methods — espresso, French press, and Turkish-style coffee — were linked to higher LDL cholesterol levels due to cafestol, a natural compound in coffee beans that is normally removed during filtration.

"Cafestol can raise LDL cholesterol by reducing the liver's ability to remove it from the bloodstream," explained Claire Cohen, a nutritional therapist at Nat-Nut Nutritional Therapy, in an interview with Medical News Today.

Adding sugar, flavored syrups, and cream also diminished coffee's health profile. "If you add too much sugar and cream, you can dilute the health benefits of coffee," Hu said. "And we have found that if you use the standard 12-ounce cup, it would be like three cups per day. Not like a big latte you get from Starbucks."

Energy Drinks Are a Different Category

The AHA explicitly separated coffee from energy drinks and energy shots. While coffee showed neutral-to-positive effects on heart health, energy drinks were tied to spikes in blood pressure and abnormal heart rhythms, particularly in younger consumers.

"Energy drinks typically contain much higher amounts of caffeine and also a very high amount of added sugar and taurine and other stimulants," Hu said. "Those kinds of drinks do not contain the potentially beneficial bioactive compounds like polyphenols." A single 16-ounce energy drink can contain 200 to 300 milligrams of caffeine — nearly the daily limit in one serving.

Dr. Amish Mehta, a cardiologist with Allegheny Health Network, told USA Today that the new guidance should reassure coffee drinkers while flagging energy drinks as the real concern. "That's where I worry more — not about a few plain coffees, but about large, concentrated energy drinks," he said.

Individual Response Still Varies

The AHA noted that age, genetics, medications, and underlying health conditions all influence how the body processes caffeine. Some individuals metabolize caffeine slowly, making them more susceptible to elevated blood pressure, palpitations, or sleep disruption even at moderate doses.

"What matters most isn't just how much coffee you drink — it's how it's prepared, what you are adding to it, and how your own body responds," said Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished. She described the statement as "reassuring, but not permissive" — evidence that moderate filtered coffee is compatible with heart health, not a prescription to drink more.
